topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Compute Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school students or curious science enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Compute Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school students or curious science enthusiasts

sections.title: Introduction: The Impossible Puzzle (1 minute)
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: A small block of mass 'm' and a large block of mass 'M = 100^n * m' on a frictionless track, with a wall on the left. We count the total number of elastic collisions. Pose the question: How does this mechanical setup relate to the digits of pi?
sections.example: Imagine a tiny hamster on a cart (mass 1) hitting a massive vault door (mass 100). The number of collisions is exactly 3.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws (1 minute)
sections.content: Briefly review elastic collision mechanics. Explain that momentum (p = mv) and kinetic energy (KE = 0.5mv^2) are conserved. Introduce the visual representation of a 'Phase Space' plot: a 2D graph where the x-axis is the velocity of the small block and the y-axis is the velocity of the large block.
sections.example: Show a vector diagram of two billiard balls hitting; use color-coded arrows to show velocity transformation before and after impact.

sections.title: The Geometry of Collisions (1.5 minutes)
sections.content: Transform the collision logic into a geometric path in the Phase Space plot. As the masses hit, their velocity vectors trace arcs along an ellipse (energy conservation) and reflect off lines (momentum conservation). Demonstrate that the number of collisions is equivalent to the number of times this path crosses a specific boundary line.
sections.example: An animation showing a 'bouncing ball' trajectory inside a circular arc wedge. Each 'clink' sound corresponds to the path crossing an invisible grid line.

sections.title: The Pi Connection: The 'Magic' Result (1 minute)
sections.content: Explain that as the ratio of mass M/m approaches infinity, the collision path approximates the circumference of a circle. By calculating the angle of the arc, we find the number of collisions maps perfectly to the digits of pi (e.g., if M = 10,000m, the answer is 31 collisions, representing 3.1).
sections.example: A visual split-screen: Left side shows blocks colliding; right side shows a digital display counting up to 31415... as the mass ratio increases.

sections.title: Conclusion: Computation through Nature (0.5 minutes)
sections.content: Summarize that this is an analog computer—using physics to solve transcendental mathematical problems. Emphasize that pi is hidden in the laws of motion.
sections.example: Closing shot: A 'Pi-Calculator' machine made of two blocks and a wall, printing the digits of pi onto a ticker-tape roll.
